implementation_notes: The standard library provides the primitives but not the striped structure: allocate a std::array<std::mutex, N> (or a heap array for large N), map keys with std::hash reduced modulo N, and guard the critical section with std::lock_guard. When one operation needs several stripes, hand the distinct mutexes to std::scoped_lock (C++17), which uses std::lock's deadlock-avoidance algorithm instead of locking them one by one. Prefer this over a map of per-key locks whenever the key domain is unbounded; use a single std::mutex when contention is not the bottleneck.
pitfalls: std::scoped_lock with the same mutex twice (two keys colliding onto one stripe) does not meet the Lockable requirements - de-duplicate stripe indices before locking.
A plain std::array<std::mutex, N> member makes the owning type non-movable; hold the stripes behind a pointer, in a static, or in a container that keeps their addresses stable.
std::hash is salted per process for some key types (e.g. std::string in libstdc++) and pointer hashes change per run; stripe placement is therefore process-local and must not be persisted.

variants.name: Reader-writer stripes with std::shared_mutex (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: When reads outnumber writes, make each stripe a std::shared_mutex (C++17): readers take shared ownership and readers hashing to the same stripe proceed in parallel, while writers take exclusive ownership and exclude everyone on that stripe. The structure is otherwise identical to the mutex array; the reader-writer bookkeeping costs more per operation, so prefer it only where reads dominate and the keyed data is genuinely read-mostly.
pitfalls: Within one thread only one lock per shared_mutex may be held at a time, so a read path needing the same stripe twice must restructure rather than nest the locks.
Shared ownership must not guard read-modify-write, insert or erase paths: those need the exclusive lock, and using shared mode there produces races that look like lost updates.
